title: Financial Policy Committee Record – April 2026
summary: The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee assessed that the Middle East conflict has created a substantial negative supply shock to the global economy, triggering significant volatility in energy prices and government bond yields while increasing the likelihood that multiple financial vulnerabilities could crystallise simultaneously. The FPC maintained the UK countercyclical capital buffer at 2% and judged that the UK banking system remains resilient and capable of supporting households and businesses through a stress.
key_points: The Middle East conflict has caused large and volatile upward moves in global energy prices and government bond yields, weighing on growth and tightening financial conditions

Global sovereign bond markets continue to see historically high issuance with higher proportions at shorter maturities, exacerbated by leverage concentrated among a small number of hedge funds pursuing similar strategies
Repo markets have functioned effectively despite high volatility and volumes, preventing a breakdown in market liquidity
Risk premia in global equity and debt markets remain compressed by historical standards, with valuations particularly stretched for US AI-focused technology companies
Private credit markets show elevated redemption requests in international retail funds, with some funds limiting redemptions, highlighting liquidity mismatch and valuation concerns
The FPC assessed that advanced AI (generative or agentic) has not yet been adopted in a manner presenting systemic risk, but risks are likely to increase as deployment expands
The Committee maintained the UK CCyB at 2%, finding banks appropriately capitalised with no evidence of lending restrictions
why_it_matters: This FPC assessment provides critical intelligence on overlapping vulnerabilities in global financial markets—sovereign debt leverage, compressed risk premia, and private credit liquidity risks—that could amplify each other if the Middle East conflict persists or worsens. Market participants managing risk and liquidity should incorporate scenarios involving sudden price adjustments into stress testing.
macro_context: The conflict represents a negative supply shock that will increase inflation and reduce growth, interacting with pre-existing vulnerabilities in sovereign debt, equity valuations, and private credit. Higher interest rates from the supply shock could increase debt-servicing pressures on leveraged borrowers.
market_structure_context: The record highlights that repo markets have functioned despite elevated volatility, preventing a liquidity crisis. However, the concentration of leverage among hedge funds using similar strategies across jurisdictions creates risk of disorderly unwind and cross-border spillovers into core sovereign bond markets.
notes: Record of FPC meeting held on 27 March 2026, published 1 April 2026. Source discusses both macro catalysts (Middle East conflict supply shock) and market structure concerns (hedge fund leverage, repo functioning, private credit liquidity). The PM SWES (Private Markets System-Wide Exploratory Scenario) is mentioned as ongoing work to explore private market risks. AI systemic risk assessment is a forward-looking element noting increasing deployment intent among regulated firms.
